annotation: It treated the filer as a qualifying surviving spouse and used joint Social Security thresholds, a joint standard deduction, and joint brackets despite no qualifying child being listed. The single-filer Social Security calculation includes $18,542.70, and the applicable itemized and senior deductions leave $26,095.78 taxable income.

It incorrectly included $48,000 of tax-exempt veterans benefits, deducted ESI premiums without wage income, and then asserted that deductions eliminated tax despite its own calculations showing substantial taxable income. The correct AGI is $50,437.11 and deductions leave $26,095.78 taxable.

It taxed 85% of Social Security rather than applying the statutory single-filer worksheet, which yields $18,542.70, and it chose the standard deduction instead of $18,341.33 of itemized deductions. Those errors raised its taxable income above the correct $26,095.78.

It assigned qualifying-surviving-spouse status without a listed qualifying child and then concluded that joint deductions reduced taxable income to zero. The filer is taxed under the single pathway, with $26,095.78 remaining after itemized and senior deductions.

Its reasoning correctly identified single status but taxed 85% of Social Security, rejected the applicable itemized deduction, and then submitted $1,176 despite deriving tax near $3,300. The correct taxable Social Security and deductions yield $26,095.78 of taxable income and $2,883.49 of tax.

It assumed qualifying-surviving-spouse status without a qualifying child, used joint Social Security thresholds and a joint standard deduction, and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction from its final arithmetic. The applicable single-filer computation instead produces $2,883.49.

It first computed about $2,023 from its stated taxable income at the 10% joint rate, then replaced that result with $3,204 using a nonexistent higher-bracket adjustment. Its submitted amount does not follow its own bracket calculation, while the applicable brackets on $26,095.78 yield $2,883.49.

It taxed the full 85% cap of Social Security and used only an aged standard deduction, omitting both the applicable $18,341.33 itemized deduction and the $6,000 senior deduction. The correct deductions reduce taxable income to $26,095.78.

It applied a TCJA-expiration regime with a personal exemption and treated ESI premiums as deductible medical expenses. The applicable 2026 computation instead uses $18,341.33 of itemized deductions plus the $6,000 senior deduction, with no personal exemption.

It stated taxable income of $37,990 but submitted only $1,109 of tax, an amount incompatible with the applicable progressive brackets. It also failed to apply the deductions that reduce taxable income to $26,095.78, on which tax is $2,883.49.

It subtracted a nonexistent 2026 personal exemption and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction while using an incomplete itemized-deduction amount. The correct deduction total is $24,341.33, leaving $26,095.78 taxable income.

It subtracted a personal exemption and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction, producing excessive taxable income. The correct total deductions are $24,341.33 and taxable income is $26,095.78.

It used a personal exemption and an incomplete itemized-deduction calculation while omitting the $6,000 senior deduction. Applying the correct $24,341.33 deduction total produces $26,095.78 of taxable income.

It correctly used single Social Security thresholds but chose an aged standard deduction after imposing an obsolete $10,000 SALT cap. The applicable itemized deductions are $18,341.33, and adding the $6,000 senior deduction reduces taxable income to $26,095.78.

It treated the aged standard deduction as large enough to offset pension, IRA, interest, and taxable Social Security income. After the applicable itemized and senior deductions, $26,095.78 remains taxable.

It used qualifying-surviving-spouse Social Security thresholds, joint deductions, and joint brackets despite the absence of a qualifying child. Single-filer treatment produces $18,542.70 of taxable Social Security and $2,883.49 of tax.

It used an aged standard deduction plus the senior deduction rather than the larger applicable itemized deduction plus senior deduction. It also misstated taxable Social Security and AGI; the trace yields $50,437.11 of AGI and $26,095.78 of taxable income.

It chose a $24,150 standard-and-senior deduction package instead of $18,341.33 of itemized deductions plus the $6,000 senior deduction. That $191.33 deduction shortfall inflated taxable income and tax above $2,883.49.

It asserted that senior deductions and credits exceeded taxable income without calculating the taxable portion of Social Security or the deduction limit. The correct computation leaves $26,095.78 taxable and has no nonrefundable credit reducing the $2,883.49 liability.

It applied a post-TCJA personal exemption and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction while using the wrong deduction structure. The applicable deductions are $18,341.33 itemized plus $6,000 senior, leaving $26,095.78 taxable income.

It improperly treated employer-sponsored premiums as deductible medical spending and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction. The correct itemized deductions are $18,341.33, and total deductions of $24,341.33 produce $2,883.49 of tax.

It chose the aged standard deduction instead of the applicable $18,341.33 itemized deduction. Including that itemized amount with the $6,000 senior deduction lowers taxable income by another $191.33 to $26,095.78.

It rejected itemizing by comparing $16,470 of property taxes with the standard deduction, omitting other trace-derived itemized amounts that bring itemized deductions to $18,341.33. Itemizing plus the $6,000 senior deduction yields $26,095.78 taxable income.

It reduced an already inconsistent tax estimate with an inapplicable lifetime-learning credit and a $750 elderly credit despite acknowledging the education credit did not apply. No nonrefundable credit offsets the tax, and the correct taxable-income computation yields $2,883.49.

All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

It also treated the mortgage balance as though it established deductible shelter expenses, even though no rent, mortgage payment, property tax, insurance, or utility expense was listed; the $44,289 gross income instead fails the threshold and yields value = 0.

It also acknowledged that household MAGI exceeds the expansion limit but then replaced the required eligibility test with a generalization that PolicyEngine typically treats low-income aged spouses as eligible.

The model incorrectly declared the couple’s $44,289 income to be well below Virginia’s aged, blind, and disabled income limit and therefore assigned an ABD pathway that the spouse does not satisfy. Minimal countable resources cannot establish ABD eligibility when the applicable categorical and income requirements are unmet.

The model treated age 69 and unspecified household information as enough to establish Medicaid eligibility without applying any pathway. The actual pathway evaluation yields category NONE: MAGI is 2.05 times FPL and no non-MAGI category applies.

The model conflated eligibility for a Medicare Savings Program with Medicaid eligibility and asserted MSP receipt without applying Virginia’s income and categorical tests. Being Medicare-aged does not establish either MSP participation or a Medicaid eligibility category, and this spouse qualifies through none.

The model incorrectly treated 40 quarters of Medicare-covered employment as a prerequisite for Medicare eligibility rather than a condition for premium-free Part A. Under the requested PolicyEngine rule, the spouse's age of 69 satisfies the age-65 Medicare eligibility criterion, so the unlisted work history does not change the result.

Virginia’s income-based age-deduction calculation does not reduce the head’s deduction dollar-for-dollar by Social Security received here; both spouses’ deductions apply and eliminate taxable income.

Excluding Social Security and subtracting both $12,000 age deductions, the joint standard deduction, and personal exemptions leaves zero Virginia taxable income.

The model substituted a $1,600 age-related addition for Virginia’s income-based age deductions of up to $12,000 per qualifying spouse. Applying the full age deductions for both spouses, rather than a small age addition, fully offsets Virginia taxable income.

The model included the household’s gross Social Security in Virginia income instead of removing Social Security and then produced mutually inconsistent taxable-income and bracket calculations. With Social Security excluded and both spouses’ age deductions plus the joint standard deduction and personal exemptions applied, Virginia taxable income is zero.
